analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal loans for manufactured home parks on basic tenant protections like rent-increase notice and lease renewal rights.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with six Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Financial Services Committee since referral with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Manufactured home residents usually own their home but rent the land underneath it, which leaves them exposed to sudden rent increases, lease non-renewals, and community sales or closures. This bill says that to get federally backed financing — loans insured by the Department of Housing and Urban Development or bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — a community owner must give residents a one-year renewable lease unless there is good cause not to renew, at least 60 days' written notice before rent increases (more notice for bigger ones), a five-day grace period on rent, the right to sell their home in place, 60 days' notice before a community is sold or closed, and a chance for tenants to negotiate to buy the community. Owners who violate the rules face losing access to federal financing for at least two years and owing payments to injured tenants. A new commission would propose stronger protections, and the bill creates a standard lease template.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities whose owners use federally backed financing — most commonly low- and moderate-income households who own their home but lease the pad site it sits on. They gain predictable lease terms, advance warning of rent hikes and community sales, and the ability to sell their home without moving it, which protects the equity in the home itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who lease their lots

how_it_helps.text: Requires one-year renewable lease terms unless there is good cause for non-renewal, plus a right against termination except for material lease violations or uniformly applied business reasons [S2][S3].

Requires at least 60 days' written notice of rent increases or new charges, with more notice for larger increases (an extra 30 days for each additional 2.5% increase above 5%), and a written justification of the increase [S2][S3].

Gives tenants a five-day grace period on rent, a 15-day right to cure defaults, the right to sell the home in place after eviction, the right to post a For Sale sign, and the right to sublease the pad site to a buyer of the home [S3].

Requires 60 days' advance notice of a community's sale or closure, with the terms of any offer disclosed and a 60-day window in which the owner must negotiate in good faith if tenants want to buy the community [S2][S3].

Attaches penalties: owners who willfully and materially violate the protections can be barred from federally backed financing for at least two years and must pay injured tenants set amounts, such as six months' rent or 125% of improperly charged rent increases with interest [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors of manufactured home communities, including large corporate and investor owners, who must either adopt the lease protections across all communities they own or give up access to HUD-insured and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac financing. Some compliance and legal costs could be passed through to tenants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Community owners, investors, and their lenders

drawbacks.text: The protections apply only to communities financed through the covered federal programs. Owners can avoid every requirement by simply not using HUD-insured or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac financing, leaving a patchwork in which many residents get nothing [S2][S3].

Because owners must apply the protections in leases at every community they own if they want federal financing for any of them, some owners may forgo federally backed credit entirely, which could raise financing costs for community purchases and rehabilitation and shrink the pool of capital keeping parks maintained rather than converted [S3].

The bill requires no new appropriations and must be administered using existing HUD and Federal Housing Finance Agency staff and funds, raising questions about how well certification and penalty enforcement would work in practice [S3].

The bill sets notice, renewal, and sale rights but does not cap rents; an owner complying with the notice rules could still raise rent substantially, though longer notice periods give households more time to respond [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents, the protections address real and common harms: owning a home you cannot easily move gives the landlord leverage that ordinary renting does not, and sudden rent increases or a community closure can wipe out a household's main asset. The bill's main design weakness is that it is voluntary in effect — it reaches only owners who want federal financing, and an owner determined to escape it can walk away from that financing. Within that narrower footprint, though, the protections are concrete, enforceable through penalties, and cannot be undercut by weaker state law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which has taken no further action on it; the bill remains alive only in the technical sense that the Congress has not yet ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brittany Pettersen introduced the bill on March 27, 2025, joined by Reps. Bonamici, Larson of Connecticut, and Tlaib, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S3][S5].
Six members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote after the initial referral [S5].

The bill would bar HUD from insuring, and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from purchasing, loans for manufactured home communities unless the borrower certifies the tenant protections and submits documentation, including its standard lease agreement, to prove compliance [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, community owners and investors: with no committee action, no new lease requirements or financing conditions have been imposed, and the financing rules remain as they were.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2025 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it stalled in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors are Democrats and there is no recorded Republican support; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill has not advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors
industries.note: Owners — including large corporate and investor buyers of parks — would have to give residents leases with renewal, notice, sale, and closure rights across every community they own, and face a two-year ban on federal financing and set payments to tenants for willful violations. Their interest in unrestricted operation of leased-pad communities runs against residents' interest in stable, predictable tenancy.

industries.industry: Multifamily lenders financing manufactured home communities (including Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac as purchasers)
industries.note: Lenders and the mortgage enterprises would lose the ability to insure or purchase loans on communities whose owners do not certify the protections, shrinking eligible deal volume, though pricing discounts would remain available for owners who go beyond the minimums. The financing industry's preference for lending without tenant-protection conditions conflicts with the protections residents would gain.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic cosponsors and no committee activity seven months into the session, the realistic path is that the bill dies at the end of the 119th Congress without a markup or vote, as most non-controversial-but-unprioritized housing bills do. A path forward would require either Democratic control of the House or a leadership decision to give the bill floor time.
